title: How a Couple Tells Its Story
text:
Kim Buehlman, John Gottman and Lynn Katz wanted to know whether the way a married couple talks about its own past could reveal where the marriage was heading. They asked couples raising young children a set of open questions in a relaxed interview: How did you meet? What attracted you to each other? What were the hard times, and how did you get through them? How has the marriage changed?

The researchers paid little attention to the facts of each story. Instead, they coded how it was told. Did the partners speak of each other with fondness and admiration, or with indifference and criticism? Did they say "we" and describe challenges they had faced together, or speak as two separate people? Did they look back on struggles with pride at getting through, or with disappointment and a sense that the marriage had not turned out as hoped? Was the story vivid and expansive, or vague and thin?

Three years later, the team checked which couples had divorced. The scores from the oral history interview alone predicted divorce with remarkable accuracy, reported at around 94 percent. Couples whose stories were full of disappointment and negativity were the ones who had split up.
lesson: Listen to how you tell the story of your relationship. Speaking with fondness and as a team keeps a bond strong; a story of disappointment is a warning.
people: Kim Buehlman, John Gottman, Lynn Katz
source: Buehlman, K. T., Gottman, J. M., and Katz, L. F. (1992). How a couple views their past predicts their future: Predicting divorce from an oral history interview. Journal of Family Psychology, 5(3-4), 295-318.
caveat: The sample was small and the high accuracy was not tested on a new group of couples, so the figure likely overstates real predictive power.
